lesson.question: Why does code that works on 10 items die on 100,000?
lesson.hook: If you’ve ever passed the sample tests and then hit "Time Limit Exceeded", you’re not alone. It happens to almost everyone, and it’s usually about growth, not speed.
lesson.plain: **Big-O** describes how the work grows as the input grows. It doesn’t time your code. It counts how many steps it needs when the input doubles.
what: O(1): same work for any size
O(n): one pass, work grows with the input
O(n²): a loop inside a loop, work explodes

problems.ask: Move all zeros to the end while keeping the order of the other numbers, in place.
hints: Write every non-zero to the front with a write pointer.
Then fill the rest with zeros.
problems.mistake: Creating a new array breaks the in-place rule.

lesson.question: How do you clean an array without making a new one?
lesson.hook: The first instinct is always "copy the good items into a new array". It works, until the problem says "in place".
lesson.plain: Use two fingers on the same array. One **reads** every item. The other **writes** only the keepers. The writer never passes the reader, so nothing unread gets overwritten.
what: A read pointer visits every item
A write pointer marks where the next keeper goes
O(1) extra space: no second array

lesson.question: How do you check if two words use the same letters?
lesson.hook: Sorting both words works, and it’s what most people try first. There’s a faster trick that only needs 26 boxes.
lesson.plain: Make 26 boxes, one per letter. For each letter, add a **tally**. A char is secretly a number, so 'c' - 'a' = 2 tells you which box.
what: int[26] is a tiny, fast map for lowercase letters
Count up for one word, down for the other
All zeros at the end means anagram

lesson.question: How do you find two numbers that add up to a target?
lesson.hook: Everyone’s first answer to Two Sum is two loops. Interviewers expect that, and then they ask: "can you do better?"
lesson.plain: Walk the list once. For each number, ask: "Have I already seen the partner I need?" Keep everything you’ve seen in a **HashMap**, so the answer is instant.
what: Partner needed = target - current number
Store number → index as you go
Check before you store, so a number can’t pair with itself

lesson.question: How do you answer 10,000 range-sum questions fast?
lesson.hook: Adding up the range every time feels natural. With thousands of questions, it quietly becomes the slowest part of your code.
lesson.plain: Do the adding once, up front. **prefix[i]** is the total of everything before position i. Then any range sum is one subtraction, like reading two odometer numbers.
what: Build once in O(n)
Each query is O(1)
A 0 at the start removes special cases

problems.ask: Find the largest sum of any path in the tree. A path can start and end anywhere.
hints: Each node returns its best one-sided path to its parent.
At each node, also try left + node + right as a complete path. Treat negative sides as 0.
problems.mistake: Starting best at 0 fails when every value is negative.

lesson.question: What’s the best path through a tree, if it can bend anywhere?
lesson.hook: This hard problem is Day 4’s diameter trick with numbers: return one thing, track another.
lesson.plain: Each node returns the best path that goes **down one side** only, because a parent can only extend one side. On the side, it checks the path that **bends** here: left + node + right. A negative side is worth 0, so you skip it.
what: Return: node + the better side
Track: left + node + right
Negative branches count as 0

research.title: Optimizers and learning rates
research.why: Half of "it doesn’t train" problems are the optimizer or the learning rate.
steps: Train your MLP with SGD, SGD with momentum, and Adam.
Try 3 learning rates for each.
Plot the loss curves side by side.

research.title: Reproduce part 1: the training loop
research.why: Copying a paper’s result is how researchers check they truly understand it.
steps: Set up a PyTorch training loop for CIFAR-10.
Build ResNet-20 as described in the paper’s CIFAR section.
Fix random seeds and log accuracy every epoch.

research.title: Reproduce part 2: plain vs residual
research.why: The paper’s key claim: a deeper plain network trains worse, and skip connections fix it.
steps: Train a plain 20-layer net and ResNet-20 with the same settings.
If time allows, add a 32-layer version of each.
Make a table: does your trend match the paper’s?
research.result: A results table vs the paper.

research.title: Your first ablation
research.why: An ablation removes one piece to see what it was doing. It’s the most common experiment in research.
steps: Pick one change: remove batch norm, or change the depth.
Run it with the same seed and settings.
Write what changed and why you think it happened.

research.title: Write it up
research.why: Research that isn’t written down doesn’t count. Professors will judge you by this write-up.
steps: Two pages: intro, method, setup, results, limitations.
Push code to GitHub with a clear README.
Add your plots and the results table.
research.result: A 2-page report and a public repo.

research.title: Find your lab
research.why: The fastest way into research is a professor at your own college.
steps: List 5 professors or labs working on vision or ML.
First-pass one recent paper from each.
Pick the 2 that excite you most.

research.title: Email a professor
research.why: A short, specific email with real work attached stands out.
steps: Use the template below and add one specific question about their paper.
Link your reproduction repo and report.
Send it to 1 or 2 professors.
research.template:
Subject: Undergraduate interested in your [topic] work

Dear Prof. [Name],

I’m [your name], a [year] student in [department]. I read your paper "[title]" and was curious about [one specific question].

To learn the field, I reproduced the CIFAR-10 results of ResNet and ran an ablation on [change]: [repo link]. A 2-page write-up is here: [link].

Would you be open to me contributing to your group, even on small tasks? I can commit [hours] a week.

Thank you for your time,
[Name]

research.title: Plan your first real experiment
research.why: Every paper lists limitations. Those are open questions you can start on.
steps: Read the limitations section of one of their papers.
Write a one-paragraph idea for a tiny experiment.
Set a weekly research slot and stick to it.
